summary.text: A telescope is a device for observing distant objects by the electromagnetic radiation they emit, absorb or reflect.
It began as an optical instrument using lenses, mirrors or both, and now covers instruments that detect other parts of the spectrum, such as radio and infrared.
The first practical ones were glass-lens refractors from the Netherlands in the early 1600s, and mirror-based reflectors followed within a few decades.

facts.label: Earliest record
facts.value: A 1608 Dutch patent by Hans Lipperhey

facts.label: First radio telescope
facts.value: A purpose-built one began operating in 1937

items.prompt: Nearly every large research telescope built since 1900 uses a mirror, not a lens, to gather light. Why?

options.label: Lens telescopes top out at about a meter across
Mirrors are always far cheaper to polish
Lenses cannot form images of faint stars
Mirrors let the telescope see through clouds

items.explain: The maximum physical size of refracting telescopes is about 1 meter, so large research telescopes have been reflectors.

items.prompt: Early astronomers wanted a curved mirror, not a lens, as the main light collector. What did a parabolic mirror promise?

options.label: Larger magnification with no need for focusing
Less spherical aberration and no chromatic aberration
Much easier polishing than glass lenses
The ability to work in full daylight

items.explain: Parabolic mirrors reduce spherical aberration and avoid chromatic aberration, which motivated many designs.

items.prompt: A team wants to image the sky in X-rays. Why does the instrument have to orbit above the ground?

options.label: X-rays are too faint to be seen at night from Earth
Ground telescopes cost too much money to build
X-rays can only be seen in total darkness
The atmosphere is opaque to most of the spectrum, X-rays included

items.explain: Only a few bands, visible through near-infrared and some radio, reach the ground, so X-ray telescopes must be in orbit.

items.prompt: Which is a real drawback of launching a telescope into space instead of building it on a mountain?

options.label: It loses the ability to see visible light
Cost, size, maintainability and upgradability suffer
It sees fewer wavelengths than a ground telescope
It gets worse views because of clouds

items.explain: Space telescopes avoid clouds and light pollution but cost more and are harder to maintain and upgrade.

items.prompt: A simple glass lens smears white light into colored fringes. What 1733 invention partially fixed this?

options.label: The achromatic lens
A larger mirror
The radio dish
Silver-coated glass

items.explain: The achromatic lens partially corrected color aberrations and allowed shorter, more functional refractors.

items.prompt: After Hans Lipperhey's patent in 1608 spread the word, how did Galileo come to observe the sky?

options.label: He bought Lipperhey's telescope outright
He invented the first one from scratch
He heard of it and built his own version
He learned the design from Newton

items.explain: The actual inventor is unknown, but word spread; Galileo heard about it and in 1609 built his own version.

paragraphs.heading: What a telescope is
paragraphs.text: A telescope lets you observe faraway objects through the electromagnetic radiation they give off, absorb or reflect. The first telescopes were optical ones, built with lenses, curved mirrors, or both. Today the word covers a wide range of instruments that pick up different parts of that spectrum.

paragraphs.heading: Lenses first, then mirrors
paragraphs.text: The first known practical telescopes were refracting telescopes, which use glass lenses, and they appeared in the Netherlands early in the 17th century. They were pointed both at the sky and at things on land. The oldest surviving record is a 1608 patent from Hans Lipperhey, a spectacle maker in Middelburg, but who truly invented it is unknown. Galileo heard the news and built his own in 1609, then used it to study objects in the sky.

paragraphs.heading: The reflecting telescope
paragraphs.text: Within a few decades came the reflecting telescope, which collects and focuses light with mirrors. Parabolic mirrors promised to reduce spherical aberration and avoid chromatic aberration, the color problems seen in lens telescopes, which led to many designs. In 1668 Isaac Newton built the first practical reflector, a design still called the Newtonian reflector. Early mirrors were made of speculum metal, which tarnished fast, until silver-coated glass arrived in 1857 and aluminized mirrors in 1932.

paragraphs.heading: Why big telescopes use mirrors
paragraphs.text: A lens-based telescope can only be built up to about 1 meter across. Because of that, most large research telescopes built since around 1900 have been reflectors. The biggest today have main mirrors more than 10 meters wide, and designs of 30 to 40 meters are in progress. A wider opening gathers more light, and it also lets the telescope pick out finer detail.

paragraphs.heading: Beyond visible light
paragraphs.text: In the 20th century, telescopes spread across the spectrum, from radio waves to gamma rays. Radio telescopes came in the 1930s, with the first purpose-built one running in 1937, and infrared telescopes followed in the 1960s. Collecting each kind of radiation takes different hardware. At longer wavelengths it gets easier to use antennas, while shorter wavelengths need mirrors the light strikes at a glancing angle.

paragraphs.heading: Going into space
paragraphs.text: Air blocks most of the electromagnetic spectrum, so only visible light, near-infrared and part of the radio range reach the ground. X-ray and far-infrared telescopes therefore have to work from orbit. Even for light that does get through, space avoids clouds, blurring from the air and light pollution. The cost is high, though, and a telescope in orbit is limited in size and hard to repair or upgrade.

paragraphs.heading: Famous examples
paragraphs.text: NASA's Hubble Space Telescope sees visible, ultraviolet and near-infrared light. The Kepler Space Telescope found thousands of planets around other stars. The James Webb Space Telescope launched on 25 December 2021 on an Ariane 5 rocket from Kourou, French Guiana. Webb sees in infrared, and it circles the L₂ Lagrange Point of the Earth–Sun system.
